messages.subject_clean: Changes to data between Stat and Geom
messages.body_plain:
I guess I'll kick things off on the new list... I'm fumbling around
with writing a new stat and geom, and I'm running into some issues.
I'm also new to the style of programming used inside of ggplot2 --
it's a big change from the user-facing R code that I'm used to working
with!

Here's my question: What happens between StatXXX$calculate and GeomYYY
$draw? If I look at the data at the end of StatXXX$calculate, it's
different from the data at the beginning of GeomYYY$draw. Between
these two phases, something is adding in columns for ymin, wmax,
weight, colour, fill, and so on. It's also modifying the values in the
y column, which is a problem for what I'm doing.

If anyone could provide a step-by-step explanation of what happens
when making a plot, that would be a really useful reference for
everyone interested in ggplot2 development.

Thanks,
-Winston

Thanks - going through ggplot_build did help me figure out what was going on. Now I have a couple other issues...

I'm writing a stat and geom for violin plots, called stat_vdensity and geom_violin. When I use position="identity", it looks OK, but when I use position="dodge" (which is currently the default), the violins are skewed. I've attached some pictures of what happens. The first is with position="dodge", the second is with "identity".

I think it's because pos_dodge() expects each row of the incoming data frame to represent one thing to dodge -- but the data frame that it's currently getting has a whole bunch of rows, each one representing one point along the edge of the polygon. It really should be the that each polygon is dodged (by its maximum width), not each row of the data frame. Any ideas how to deal with this?

I'm also running into an issue where this works (the default geom for stat_vdensity is "violin"):
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + stat_vdensity()

But this gives me an error:
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin()
# Error: No stat called vdensity

For stat_vdensity, I adapted the code from stat_density, and far as I can tell, I've replaced every instance of "density" with "vdensity", but apparently I haven't registered the name somewhere that I need to.

Thanks in advance for help!
-Winston

messages.body_plain:
I've figured out a way to deal with the issue of dodging polygon-based geoms, by modifying pos_dodge().

The original version of pos_dodge expects each dodged item to be represented on one row of the incoming "data" data frame. For geom_boxplot, it might look something like this:

 ymin  lower middle upper ymax           outliers x fill PANEL group weight   xmin   xmax
-1.28 -0.740 -0.310  0.31 1.29 -3.40, -2.83, 1.89 1    A     1     1      1 0.9625 1.0375
-1.82 -0.305  0.465  0.84 2.23                2.6 1    B     1     2      1 0.9625 1.0375

For a polygon-based geom like a violin plot, the incoming data to pos_dodge might look like this:
   vdensity       y     scaled      count width x fill PANEL group ymin ymax xmin xmax
 0.04766652 -3.4000 0.13004358  1.4299956   0.5 1    A     1     1 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.01023525 -2.0775 0.02792375  0.3070574   0.5 1    A     1     1 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.36654266 -0.7550 1.00000000 10.9962798   0.5 1    A     1     1 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.30788010  0.5675 0.83995707  9.2364030   0.5 1    A     1     1 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.04685905  1.8900 0.12784065  1.4057716   0.5 1    A     1     1 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.13080369 -1.8200 0.30726116  3.9241107   0.5 1    B     1     2 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.13900456 -0.7150 0.32652521  4.1701368   0.5 1    B     1     2 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.42570851  0.3900 1.00000000 12.7712553   0.5 1    B     1     2 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.17094522  1.4950 0.40155463  5.1283567   0.5 1    B     1     2 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25
 0.06616696  2.6000 0.15542785  1.9850088   0.5 1    B     1     2 -3.4  2.6 0.75 1.25

This represents two simplified violin polygons for A and B. The pre-dodging bounding rectangle is represented by ymin, ymax, xmin, and xmax. At this stage, the points of the polygon haven't been computed yet; they'll be generated from the "y" and "scaled".

To dodge the geoms, instead of assuming each row is one object, I have it break it up by the value of "group", and then dodge each group.

A couple questions:
- Is it correct to assume that each separate object always will have a different group number?
- geom_boxplot uses a list to represent all outliers on one row of the data frame. Would it be better to store the polygon's x and y coordinates as a list this way?

It seems to me that using the group number to identify each object is a better solution than using each row to identify an object (the latter would require stuffing each row with lots of coordinates), but there may be something important I'm missing.

I'll try to get my code up on github soon...

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
The branch is here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/tree/feature/violin

A couple comments about the changes made to pos_dodge() in position-collide.r to use a bounding box:
- It assumes (without checking) that within each group, xmin and xmax are always the same. This is probably OK because the caller function, collide(), checks that xmin and xmax are the same, not just within each group, but across all entries in the data frame.
- It dodges each group the same amount. For example, if there are three groups, it allocates 1/3 of the total width to each. It would be possible to modify it to dodge objects of different widths according to their size, though collide() would have to be changed to allow different values of xmin and xmax.

I haven't yet modified pos_stack() or pos_fill() to work with the bounding boxes.

-Winston

messages.subject: geom_violin
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone - I have a rough working version of geom_violin. Comments and suggestions are appreciated.

https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/tree/feature/violin

Some examples -- hopefully these inline images will show up properly...

set.seed(110)
dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=round(rnorm(90),2))

# With points overlaid
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin() + geom_point(shape=21)

# Narrower, no points
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin(width=.5)

# Narrower, with tails
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin(width=.5, trim=FALSE) + geom_point(shape=21)

# With box plot
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin(width=.5) + geom_boxplot(width=.1, outlier.size=0)

# Dodging works
ggplot(dat, aes(x="foo", y=y, fill=x)) + geom_violin()

Dennis, thanks for the feedback. Here's an example with jitter:

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_violin() +

    geom_point(shape=21, position=position_jitter(height=0, width=.2))

I think the next thing I'm going to do is implement a Wilkinson-style dot plot. I posted some code on the main ggplot2 list a little while back to make make this kind of graph, but it wasn't very elegant -- it required using a continuous x axis. Here's what it looks like using that hack:

I think this is way more informative than jittering. I just have to figure out a good way to do it. It's kind of complicated because of the way dot size is related to the binning and axis dimensions. With "regular" point graphs, the dot diameter is independent of the axis dimensions, but with a Wilkinson-style dot plot, the dot diameter determines the bin size.

I'm hoping that I can use geom_point with a new position_xx and/or stat_xx, but if not, I'll have to make a new geom.

-Winston

> > It seems to me that using the group number to identify each object is a
> > better solution than using each row to identify an object (the latter would
> > require stuffing each row with lots of coordinates), but there may be
> > something important I'm missing.
>
> No, that sounds like a really good idea. It would also let you use
> dodging to adjust geom_point to line up groups of points with error
> bars.

I've also updated pos_stack() to stack by group rather than by each row of incoming data.

> I also like the idea of thinking about a bounding box.  Maybe that
> should be a geom method.

I've made some changes to collide() and pos_dodge() so that it allows dodging items of unequal width.
- In collide(), I removed the check for unequal width (duh) and also for overlapping xmin-xmax intervals. I'm not 100% sure that this won't cause unexpected problems, but it seemed OK for the stuff I was trying out.
- The dodging works by allocating a total width equal to the average of xmax-xmin for all the objects. In the example I've attached, the starting width of each object is .9, .9, and 1.8, so the average width is 1.2. It then fits all the objects in that total width, and centers it over the x position.

Another possible way to do the space allocation is to fit the objects all into the specified width (usually .9), but that may require slightly more extensive modifications.

> Would you mind starting to write a few tests for colliding?  That will
> at least start to formally describe the expected behaviour in the
> tests that you're doing.  Calling collide with data directly would be
> most helpful I think.

Sure, I can do that.

There are a few different sets of assumptions I could make about the values of xmin, xmax, ymin, and ymax (I'll call these the bounding vars) in the data going into collide().
1. Leave things as-is. This eliminates the need for modifying the geoms, but there seems to be some inconsistency in how the bounding vars are used, as Kohske noted in bug 274. It also makes things a little messier inside of collide().
2. Make sure that all data going into collide() has ymin and ymax set when using stack and fill, and has xmin and xmax set when using dodge. If I make this change to collide, then I think some geoms will break, but I'm guessing that won't be too hard to fix.
3. Make sure that all data going into collide() has all the bounding vars set, so each object has a full bounding rectangle. This will probably require modifying a lot of geoms.

Which do you think should be used?

If you want (3), you could also go a step further and change all geoms so that they have a full bounding rectangle -- even those geoms that will never go into collide(). Perhaps the rectangle would be useful for other purposes?

> > I've made some changes to collide() and pos_dodge() so that it allows
> > dodging items of unequal width.
> > - In collide(), I removed the check for unequal width (duh) and also for

> > then fits all the objects in that total width, and centers it over the x
> > position.
>
> What happens if they have overlapping xmin-xmax ranges?  Do they get modified?

If I understand your question right, the previously attached example has this property -- two of the objects started having values of xmin=.55 and xmax=1.45, while the third object had xmin=.1 and xmax=1.9. In this case, they did get modified.

If they're overlapping but off-center, I think this is what happens, though I haven't tested it yet. Suppose you have two objects, with x ranges [7,10] and [8,17]. Before scaling, the objects have width 3 and 9, for a summed width of 12. The objects therefore have 1/4 and 3/4 of the width. They'll be scaled to fit in the full range of the original objects, [7,17], which has a total width of 10, so after scaling, they'll have width 2.5 and 7.5. They'll also be centered about the center of the original range [7,17], which is 12. So the final x ranges will be [7, 9.5] and [9.5, 17]. Does that sound like a reasonable way to do it?

-Winston

messages.subject: Coordinates and stacking/dodging
messages.body_plain:
I have some more thoughts about coordinates and stacking/dodging that I thought I'd share... I'll list these in order from concrete to abstract. I guess most of these might be more appropriate for 1.0.

1.
The behavior of pos_stack() is currently undefined when ymin!=0. Here are two possible ways to define it: The objects could either be stacked with 0 as the baseline, or using the smallest ymin value of all the objects. In either case, it would be useful to have an option for stacking downward from the largest ymax, as with stacked bar or area graphs with negative values. I believe that stacking for negative values is also not well-defined right now. (Maybe this one is appropriate for 0.9.0?)

2.
The variables x and y seem to not be well-defined. They represent the data values in some cases, but are also sometimes used for geometric properties, in ways that aren't always consistent with the data. For example, x initially means the x position of the data; but after pos_dodge, it's modified to the value (xmin+xmax)/2, which is the center of the of the geometric object. If the meaning of x is supposed to change, it would be helpful to have definitions like, "at stage A, x means this, and at stage B, x means that." Or if the data x is different from the geom's x, perhaps there should be two different variables.

Same goes for ymin, ymax, etc. One option is to have these values represent the bounding box of objects. Presently they're also sometimes used to describe the data -- it's conceivable that a geom would have a bounding box that is larger or smaller than the ymin and ymax of the data. And sometimes the a single object has many values of ymin and ymax: with geom_ribbon, ymin and ymax represent the range at each x value, not the bounding box of the whole ribbon.

(Incidentally, I'll probably have to revert the changes I made to pos_stack because my version operates on the bounding box, which won't work correctly with stacked area graphs.)

3.
This brings me back to stacking and dodging. Stack, dodge, and fill can be generalized to a single function with a bunch of options.

There's one more issue I should mention before describing the function. When dodging polygons, sometimes you want to stack/dodge by bounding rectangle (as with the violin plots), and sometimes you want to stack/dodge by each vertex of the polygon (as with stacked area graphs).

Here's a sketch of a function, uncollide() that generalizes across all the existing cases. It has the following parameters:
- direction: "x" or "y"
- bounds: "rectangle" for uncolliding based on bounding box, "polygon" for uncolliding based on the polygon (like a stacked area graph).
- position: "center", "stackup", or "stackdown"
- baseline: the desired baseline for stacking. "min" for the using the minimum x/y value of the objects, "max" for the max value, or a numerical value.
- rescale: what to do with scaling the objects after uncolliding. "none" for no change in size, "fit" for scaling to fit original span, or a numerical value.

As currently written, pos_stack is equivalent to:
uncollide(direction="y", bounds="polygon", position="stackup", baseline=0, rescale="none")

pos_dodge is equivalent to:
uncollide(direction="x", bounds="rectangle", position="center", rescale="fit")

pos_fill is equivalent to:
uncollide(direction="y", bounds="polygon", position="stackup", baseline=0, rescale=1)

A Wilkinson-style dot plot might use this:
uncollide(direction="x", bounds="rectangle", position="center", rescale="none")

With this general solution, there are probably some other sets of parameters that would be useful that I haven't thought of yet.

-Winston

messages.subject: Notched boxplots
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I just made an implementation of notched box plots. There are two new parameters for geom_boxplot:
- notch = TRUE/FALSE
- notchwidth = the relative width of the notch to the overall width (default .5)

set.seed(110)
dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=round(rnorm(90),2))

# Notched box plot
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE)

# Can set notch width
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE, notchwidth=.2)

# Manually-specified positions
ggplot(NULL, aes(x = 1, y=NULL, ymin = 0, lower = 25, middle = 50,
                 upper = 75, ymax = 100, notchupper=60, notchlower=40)) +
  geom_boxplot(stat="identity", notch=TRUE)

# Gives a warning if notches go past hinges
ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) + geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE) + ylim(10,35)
# Warning messages:1: In get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...) :
#   notch went outside hinges. Try setting notch=FALSE.
# 2: In get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...) :
#   notch went outside hinges. Try setting notch=FALSE.

# Regular boxplot function gives similar warning
boxplot(mpg ~ cyl, mtcars, notch=TRUE)
# Warning message:
# In bxp(list(stats = c(21.4, 22.8, 26, 30.4, 33.9, 17.8, 18.65, 19.7,  :
#   some notches went outside hinges ('box'): maybe set notch=FALSE

(You may have noticed that the outliers are different between geom_boxplot and the base boxplot. This is a known issue with geom_boxplot.)

It also supports weighted boxplots. Normally the notch size is:
  median +- 1.58*IQR*sqrt(n)
Where n is the number of observations. Weighted boxplots require a change to the calculation of n, so it uses the sum of all weights at observations where weight and y values are not NA. For example, three unweighted observations at a given y value are the same as one observation with weight=3, in terms of calculating notch size.

It required some changes to geom_crossbar; instead of drawing the body with a GeomRect, it now uses GeomPolygon.

https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/commit/4f3356e5d6030c39c0b388aa3d073211cf6cefcb

As usual, comments and suggestions are welcome!
-Winston

> > 3.
> > This brings me back to stacking and dodging. Stack, dodge, and fill can be
> > generalized to a single function with a bunch of options.
> >
> > There's one more issue I should mention before describing the function. When
> > dodging polygons, sometimes you want to stack/dodge by bounding rectangle
> > (as with the violin plots), and sometimes you want to stack/dodge by each
> > vertex of the polygon (as with stacked area graphs).
> >
> > Here's a sketch of a function, uncollide() that generalizes across all the
> > existing cases. It has the following parameters:
> > - direction: "x" or "y"
> > - bounds: "rectangle" for uncolliding based on bounding box, "polygon" for
> > uncolliding based on the polygon (like a stacked area graph).
> > - position: "center", "stackup", or "stackdown"
> > - baseline: the desired baseline for stacking. "min" for the using the
> > minimum x/y value of the objects, "max" for the max value, or a numerical
> > value.
> > - rescale: what to do with scaling the objects after uncolliding. "none" for
> > no change in size, "fit" for scaling to fit original span, or a numerical
> > value.
> >
> > As currently written, pos_stack is equivalent to:
> > uncollide(direction="y", bounds="polygon", position="stackup", baseline=0,
> > rescale="none")
> >
> > pos_dodge is equivalent to:
> > uncollide(direction="x", bounds="rectangle", position="center",
> > rescale="fit")
> >
> > pos_fill is equivalent to:
> > uncollide(direction="y", bounds="polygon", position="stackup", baseline=0,
> > rescale=1)
> >
> > A Wilkinson-style dot plot might use this:
> > uncollide(direction="x", bounds="rectangle", position="center",
> > rescale="none")
>

> outside of ggplot so it is easy to use for other graphics packages and
> working up a set of graphical demonstrations.  That would really help
> me understand what you're thinking too.  (And also if you're
> interested, I think this sort of work is publishable)
>

messages.subject: Dot plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I've written an implementation of dot plots. It required creating a new grob, which I called dotcluster. Because of the way the dots have to be stacked, the dotcluster grob acts somewhat differently from other objects used in ggplot2.

There are two binning algorithms: "histodot", which is the same as "stat_bin" but with modifications to bin along x or y, and "dotdensity" (the default), which is taken from Wilkinson (1999). To use geom_dotplot, you set the bin width, and it scales the dots so that the diameter is the same as the bin width. (With the dotdensity algorithm, the bin width is really the maximum bin width.)

It's still a work in progress... if you feel like testing it out, please let me know if you run into problems or how it can be improved.
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/tree/feature/wdotplot

Some notes:
- With dot density binning, dot stacks can overlap with each other, by up to 50% of the dot width.
- Stacking is by dot diameter, not by y coordinate. This means that when you resize the window, the dots stay visually stacked, while the y axis might change. Circles have the same x and y dimensions in visual space, but not in the data space.
- When binning along the x axis, each dot has a y coordinate (and ymin and ymax) so that the range of the y axis is set. However, the dots aren't actually placed at that y coordinate -- they're stacked visually. Each stack of dots can be thought of as a single object which, like a text object, doesn't change dimensions when you change the y scaling.
- When binning along y axis (and stacking along x), the stack of dots is assigned a total width of 'width', usually 0.9. This is to allow for dodging. I tried adding an option so that each dot in a stack gets an incremented x value (1, 2, 3), but the scale system didn't seem to like me messing with x values like that. It also didn't like when I used just aes(y=y), without setting x or mapping something to x. I don't know if there's a way to deal with it

Issues I haven't figured out yet:
- Should it be called something other than "dotplot", to distinguish it from Cleveland dot plots?
- When stacking on y, instead of setting the y values of each dot to 1, 2, 3, should I just treat the whole stack as an object with height=1?
- I think the dot density binning algorithm is right, but there may be trouble cases that I haven't encountered yet. He mentions some sort of smoothing algorithm that takes a final pass over the bins, but I haven't implemented it.
- Coord transforms don't work. At this point I don't know if they even make sense conceptually for these objects.

Problems:
- Right now, if you want to bin along the y axis (instead of the default x), you have to set binaxis="x" and binstataxis="x". The reason for this is because I can't figure out how to give one parameter to both the stat_bindot and GeomDotplot. It looks like the way things are coded, stats "eat up" parameters so that they're not available for the geom.

In Wilkinson's grammar of graphics book, he gives specifications of these of dot plots. However, they have some characteristics that seem to violate the GoG -- at least, if you treat each dot as an object with x and y coordinates. If you treat each stack as a single object, then it might make more sense, but then position adjustments like dodging are problematic. I'll have to think about this some more. If someone wants to enlighten me, I'd appreciate it!

At any rate, on to the fun stuff, the examples and pictures. Here are some graphs I've been using for testing.

set.seed(122)
dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(20), y=rnorm(20))

# Stack vertically, sitting on 0 as baseline.
dp1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x)) + geom_rug() + scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=.2, colour="red")
# Notice each dot stack is centered over a set of observations. The binning is done with
# Wilkinson's (1999) dot density algorithm. 'binwidth' sets the maximum bin width.
# The y range is correctly set from 0 to 5, but the y axis scale actually has nothing
# to do within y positioning of the dots. The dot diameter is the same as the maximum
# bin width and they're stacked visually; if you resize the window to make it taller
# or shorter, they stay visually stacked. You could resize the window so that the dots
# align with the tick marks

# Use histodot binning
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=.2, colour="red", binmethod="histodot")
# This uses the algorithm from stat_bin: with fixed-width intervals.

# Squish together vertically with smaller stackratio
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, stackratio=.8)

# Stacking methods (stackdir="up" is default)
# stack down
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="down")

# stack center
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="center")

# stack centerwhole
# keep dots aligned and add one dot up, then one down, then one up, etc.
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="centerwhole")

# stack centerwholedown - reverse of centerwhole
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="centerwholedown")

# Dot diameter expanded to 1.4 * max binwidth.
# Stacking remains so that they're just touching vertically
dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1,colour="black", dotsize=1.4)

# Bin along Y
dp1y <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=0, y=y)) + geom_rug() + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
dp1y +  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="center")
# Notice that 'binaxis' and 'binstataxis' need to be set.

# Y direction, stack centerwhole
dp1y +  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="centerwhole")

# Data with x and g as factors
dat2 <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=round(rnorm(90),2), g=LETTERS[1:2])

# Groups on x axis
dp2 <- ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
dp2 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.25, colour="black", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
                   stackdir="centerwhole")

# Groups on x axis with violins (also smaller bin size)
dp2 + geom_violin() +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.15, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
               stackdir="center")

# With boxplots and violins, also violin width scaled relative to each other
dp2 + geom_violin(fullwidth=FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(position="dodge", width=.2, outlier.size=0) +
  geom_dotplot(alpha=.3, binwidth=.15, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
               stackdir="center")

# Dodging, mapping "x" to fill instead of x
ggplot(dat2, aes(x="foo", y=y, fill=x)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.25, alpha=.4, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
               stackdir="centerwhole")

# grouping on x and g, dodging
ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=g)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, alpha=.2, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
               stackdir="centerwhole")
# These clusters don't have an "real" x width, so dodging is a bit weird. In this case
# the clusters are too close together, but if you just make the window wider, the clusters
# will move apart (within each cluster the dots will stay together).

# Vertical, with grouping on x and g, with boxplots and violins
ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
  geom_violin(aes(colour=g), fill="white") +
  geom_boxplot(aes(colour=g), position=position_dodge(0.9),
               width=.3, outlier.size=0) +
  geom_dotplot(aes(fill=g), binwidth=.15, alpha=.3,  position="dodge",
               binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="center")

> In Wilkinson's grammar of graphics book, he gives specifications of these of dot plots. However, they have some characteristics that seem to violate the GoG -- at least, if you treat each dot as an object with x and y coordinates. If you treat each stack as a single object, then it might make more sense, but then position adjustments like dodging are problematic. I'll have to think about this some more. If someone wants to enlighten me, I'd appreciate it!
>
>
> At any rate, on to the fun stuff, the examples and pictures. Here are some graphs I've been using for testing.
>
>
> set.seed(122)
> dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(20), y=rnorm(20))
>
> # Stack vertically, sitting on 0 as baseline.
> dp1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x)) + geom_rug() + scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=.2, colour="red")
> # Notice each dot stack is centered over a set of observations. The binning is done with
> # Wilkinson's (1999) dot density algorithm. 'binwidth' sets the maximum bin width.
> # The y range is correctly set from 0 to 5, but the y axis scale actually has nothing
> # to do within y positioning of the dots. The dot diameter is the same as the maximum
> # bin width and they're stacked visually; if you resize the window to make it taller
> # or shorter, they stay visually stacked. You could resize the window so that the dots
> # align with the tick marks
>
>
>
> # Use histodot binning
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=.2, colour="red", binmethod="histodot")
> # This uses the algorithm from stat_bin: with fixed-width intervals.
>
>
> # Squish together vertically with smaller stackratio
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, stackratio=.8)
>
>
> # Stacking methods (stackdir="up" is default)
> # stack down
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="down")
>
>
> # stack center
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="center")
>
>
>
> # stack centerwhole
> # keep dots aligned and add one dot up, then one down, then one up, etc.
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="centerwhole")
>
>
>
> # stack centerwholedown - reverse of centerwhole
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1, stackdir="centerwholedown")
>
>
> # Dot diameter expanded to 1.4 * max binwidth.
> # Stacking remains so that they're just touching vertically
> dp1 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, alpha=1,colour="black", dotsize=1.4)
>
>
> # Bin along Y
> dp1y <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=0, y=y)) + geom_rug() + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
> dp1y +  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="center")
> # Notice that 'binaxis' and 'binstataxis' need to be set.
>
>
>
> # Y direction, stack centerwhole
> dp1y +  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.4, binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="centerwhole")
>
>
> # Data with x and g as factors
> dat2 <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=round(rnorm(90),2), g=LETTERS[1:2])
>
> # Groups on x axis
> dp2 <- ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4))
> dp2 + geom_dotplot(binwidth=.25, colour="black", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
>                    stackdir="centerwhole")
>
>
>
> # Groups on x axis with violins (also smaller bin size)
> dp2 + geom_violin() +
>   geom_dotplot(binwidth=.15, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
>                stackdir="center")
>
>
> # With boxplots and violins, also violin width scaled relative to each other
> dp2 + geom_violin(fullwidth=FALSE) +
>   geom_boxplot(position="dodge", width=.2, outlier.size=0) +
>   geom_dotplot(alpha=.3, binwidth=.15, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
>                stackdir="center")
>
>
>
> # Dodging, mapping "x" to fill instead of x
> ggplot(dat2, aes(x="foo", y=y, fill=x)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
>   geom_dotplot(binwidth=.25, alpha=.4, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
>                stackdir="centerwhole")
>
>
> # grouping on x and g, dodging
> ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=g)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
>   geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, alpha=.2, position="dodge", binaxis="y", binstataxis="y",
>                stackdir="centerwhole")
> # These clusters don't have an "real" x width, so dodging is a bit weird. In this case
> # the clusters are too close together, but if you just make the window wider, the clusters
> # will move apart (within each cluster the dots will stay together).
>
>
>
> # Vertical, with grouping on x and g, with boxplots and violins
> ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
>   geom_violin(aes(colour=g), fill="white") +
>   geom_boxplot(aes(colour=g), position=position_dodge(0.9),
>                width=.3, outlier.size=0) +
>   geom_dotplot(aes(fill=g), binwidth=.15, alpha=.3,  position="dodge",
>                binaxis="y", binstataxis="y", stackdir="center")
>

messages.body_plain:
This thread started over on the ggplot2 users group, I'm moving it
here at Hadley's request and will state the problem fresh and I hope,
clearly.

I have a package called HandyStuff which worked fine under R 2.13.1
but has problems under R 2.14.0.  The package is over at Github
(github.com/bryanhanson/HandyStuff <http://github.com/bryanhanson/HandyStuff>) if you care to inspect any detail
of it.

The problem is perhaps most easily illustrated by what happens when I
try to run an example from the function called compareCats.  Appended
below is my console output beginning from a fresh boot of R, then
proceeding to try some examples.  Note that various function names are
being overwritten at different points,  though none seem to be part of
the problem (at least to me).  The first error is that R can't find
the function position_jitter which is definitely exported.  Then after
I deliberately load ggExtra, R can't find the function layer which
seems rather fundamental!

I would add that if I modify the example to change arguments, which
puts me into a different part of the function, sooner or later an
error occurs which claims a certain ggplot2 function can't be found
(e.g. change freckles = FALSE and re-run then it can't find
stat_summary  Trying ?stat_summary at this point finds no page.  Doing
library(ggplot2) and then ?stat_summary finds the page.  Retrying the
example now works!  So something is not loading right.

I am pretty certain that the problem is the result of ggplot2 being
"loaded via namespace" as opposed to being "attached".  I had this
problem with mvbutils and was only able to solve it by having
library(mvbutils) in my .Rprofile

I also tried to use the develop version of ggplot2, but that does not
currently load for me (I put that transcript all the way at the
bottom).  But I don't think this is the problem.

Perhaps I misunderstand what is supposed to happen when one imports a
package during installation, but I don't think this should behave this
way.

Thanks for any pointers.  Sorry this is so long.  I hope it has the
info needed to troubleshoot.  Bryan

Hi,

I've removed ggExtra from googlecode and r-forge; this experimental
package had become redundant and unreliable with the upcoming version
of ggplot2.
I'll consider starting a new version from scratch, on github, after I
become more familiar with the new framework of ggplot2. I believe
there is a niche for sharing experimental code, geoms, themes and add-
ons aside from the core ggplot2 development.

Looking forward to the Christmas release of ggplot2 :)

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Fixed in https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/commit/faded39f7e4582c3a062eb1a85765e75c55aff25.
 The problem was in how the components of the plot were getting
combined - the width of the strips overrode the panel widths and
caused problems.

I discovered this by using gtable_show_layout on each of the gtable
objects until I discovered the point at which the correct sizing was
lost, and then noticed I'd made similar fix for axes.

Thanks for the bug report!

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Maybe this if off-topic for off-topic, but I'm thinking about table axis.
Please find the attached picture. This was semi-manually done, though.
Probably I came across this feature request in SO or ggplot2 list.

The tableGrob in gridExtra is nice, but one request:
Is it possible to implement an interface for setting width/height of
each row/column?
Now the w/h is determined based on the contents. So it is not easy to
align the panel.

Just note that more general idea about guide-positional framework,
analogous to guide legend and guide colourbar:

input: positional information of breaks of main panel, and
supplementary information.
output: a grob aligned to the main panel.

Now there is only one guide-positional, i.e. guide-axis.
Other two guides are in my brain, guidep-table and guidep-marginal.
The attached picture represents gudip-table.
guidep-marginal will look like this:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/8545035/scatterplot-with-marginal-histograms-in-ggplot2

But long afterward, anyway.

kohske

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Please consider this example:
```
# data.frame has appropriate name for aes.df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y
= 1:3, label = letters[1:3])
# works, but redundant.ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
geom_text()```
Obviously it looks redundant.
```ggplot(df, aes()) + geom_text()ggplot(df, aes_identity()) +
geom_text()ggplot(df, aes_map()) + geom_text()```It is nice if aes can
automatically map the variable name into the aes of that name.Or,
maybe I miss some existing function?
--

messages.subject: Re: automatics aes mapping from data.frame
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the comment. So I just wrote something.

aes_auto <- function(data = NULL, ...) {
  # detect names of data
  if (is.null(data)) {
    stop("aes_auto requires data.frame or names of data.frame.")
  } else if (is.data.frame(data)) {
    vars <- names(data)
  } else {
    vars <- data
  }

  # automatically detected aes
  vars <- intersect(.all_aesthetics, vars)
  names(vars) <- vars
  aes <- lapply(vars, function(x) parse(text=x)[[1]])

  # explicitly defined aes
  if (length(match.call()) > 2) {
    aes <- c(aes, as.list(match.call()[-(1:2)]))
  }

  structure(aes, class = "uneval")
}

#test codes.

df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3, colour = 1:3, label = letters[1:3])

aes_auto(df)
aes_auto(names(df))

df <- data.frame(xp = 1:3, y = 1:3, colour = 1:3, txt = letters[1:3], foo = 1:3)

aes_auto(df, x = xp, label = txt)
aes_auto(names(df), x = xp, label = txt)

df <- data.frame(foo = 1:3)
aes_auto(df, x = xp, y = yp)
aes_auto(df)

What do you think?

OK, here's what I've been doing. At Hadley's suggestion, I installed
SmartGit for use on my Win 7 system a while back. I've been able to pull the
ggplot2 and scales packages (as well as a couple of others) for almost
a month now from Hadley's repositories. The other day I started making
changes to the
documentation in ggplot2 per an item on the ggplot2 issues board. To
do that, I created a local branch (document12.22) to make changes. I
now have a number of modified files to which I have made commits in
that branch and locally reinstalled ggplot2 to check the documentation.

After going through this a few times, I finally got a clean check_doc.
I decided to try to push the commits to the remote repository from
which I had made a clone in SmartGit (Hadley's ggplot2 master
directory) but Github wanted a user id and password. After a couple of
false starts, I tried my own, but got a failure notice (not too
surprisingly). The problem is that I'm trying to push changes to someone
else's repository.

After this discussion, I infer the game is to:
    * fork Hadley's ggplot2 repository to my Github account
    * clone the forked repository to my computer
    * make changes
    * push changes back to my local repository on Github
    * send a pull request to Hadley.

Is that right?

>From this help page on Github http://help.github.com/fork-a-repo/, I
was able to successfully fork the ggplot2 repository to my Github user
account and then clone it to my computer in SmartGit under new names.

Is there anything I have to do to ensure that Hadley can pull material
from my repository once I make changes that I'd like to push, or does
the pull request handle that automatically? It appears to be
automatic, but I just want to check.

TIA,
Dennis

PS: Apologies to Jake for sending an incomplete version of this to him
inadvertently.

messages.subject_clean: Wiki page for ggplot2 development with github
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

There's been a lot of discussion recently about how to work with github, so I made a wiki page about it here:

https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Developing-ggplot2-with-github

Let me know what you think.

Hadley, I can move this to your ggplot2 wiki if you think that would be a good place.

I was thinking of adding a section about how to go about doing development, but I don't know if I'm doing in a particularly good way. My tools are basically just "load_all('ggplot2/')", options(error=recover), and a lot of print statements because the stack traces are often impossible to understand. (I think this is because of proto?)

-Winston

Thanks, Winston. Very well organized and well written.

I managed to fork the ggplot2 repository and clone it to my computer,

$ git remote add hadley git://github.com/hadley/ggplot2.git <http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2.git>
fatal: Not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git

I finally found the ggplot2 directory cloned from the Git Bash
command, so one less worry.

I managed to clone my two repositories in SmartGit (ggplot2 and
scales) and assign them new names to distinguish them from Hadley's
repositories. The question from there is how to do the equivalent of
git remote add in SmartGit. I looked around, but didn't find anything
in the menus that would do the job. Perhaps someone with experience in
SmartGit can help with that - the only thing I can think of is to pull
a repository from Hadley's account, merge it with the one I cloned,
write changes in a new branch and then push that to my Github
repository, but that seems like a lot of unnecessary work. I suspect
there's an easier way.

Dennis

It looks like I forgot to add "cd ggplot2" after the git clone. I've fixed it in the wiki.

> I managed to clone my two repositories in SmartGit (ggplot2 and

> write changes in a new branch and then push that to my Github
> repository, but that seems like a lot of unnecessary work. I suspect
> there's an easier way.

In general, I'm not sure how to do these things on Windows... IIRC, msysgit includes a bash shell where you can run git from the command line. Even if you don't do that all the time, you'll probably eventually run into cases where it's necessary. All the help out there is written for the command line.

If anyone out there is experienced with using git in Windows, please feel free to update the wiki page.

One alternative you may want to look into is to do your development in a Linux virtual machine, using VirtualBox. I've been using Ubuntu in a VM, and it has some advantages: there are excellent free text editors (like geany) and all the development software you need is available with a simple "apt-get install xxx"

-Winston

messages.subject: ggplotGrob
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There doesn't seem to be a direct equivalent of ggplotGrob in the new
version of ggplot2. I needed that function for grid.arrange() in the
gridExtra package, which can place various kinds of grobs on a page
(lattice, ggplot, raw grid, ...). I've been using the following trick,

ggplotGrob <- function(x)
ggplot2:::gtable_gTree(ggplot2:::ggplot_gtable(ggplot2:::ggplot_build(x)))

messages.subject: Layers package
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I wanted to point you all to the layers package,
https://github.com/hadley/layers, where I'm experimenting with the
future implementation of geoms, stats, position adjustments (adjusts)
and layers for ggplot2.  Layers is currently a separate package so I
can experiment with the best interface without the baggage of the
existing ggplot2 implementation, but it will eventually be integrated
back into ggplot2 (definitely by 1.0).

The main aim is to improve the implementation of these important
ggplot2 objects:

* switching from proto to S3
* documenting the generics
* splitting out big complicated methods into smaller simpler methods
* using a more efficient data structure (lists instead of data frames)
* making them easier to test
* making them easier to document

and generally making it easier to create new geoms, stats and adjusts.

Currently, only the interface for geoms is developed enough for
feedback, so if you're interested, I'd really appreciate your comments
on the design.  Start with geom.r, reading the source code for
geom_plot to understand the basic sequence of method calls, then read
the documentation for the generics, and the implementations of various
geoms in geom-*.r

The definition of geoms is a bit cleaner in layers - geom_bar really
represents a bar geometric object, not a layer that uses geom_bar,
stat_identity and position_identity. I'm not sure how this will end up
in ggplot2, but eventually I would like to replace (e.g.)
geom_histogram with layer_histogram, reserving geoms for real
geometric objects. I don't see an easy way to do this without breaking
a large amount of existing code, so there will either be a length
period where both work, or I'll have to make ggplot3 :/

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject_clean: A few things from running the examples in the ggplot2 book
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley:

I ran the examples in the ggplot2 book the other day and just
rechecked the ones I flagged after installing the latest devel version
a few minutes ago. It's not a long list, fortunately.

## Issue 1:  comma_format() doesn't always work in a plot call. Here's
an example (not unique, BTW) from Ch. 3:

library('ggplot2')
library('scales')
set.seed(1410) # Make the sample reproducible
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]

### dollar format fails:
q <- qplot(carat, price, data = dsmall,
  ylab = "Price ($)", xlab = "Weight (carats)",
  main = "Price-weight relationship"
  )
q + scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar)
Error in if (max(x) < 100) 2 else 0 :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

################################
## Issue 2: warning with an empty plot:

df <- data.frame(
   x = c(3, 1, 5),
   y = c(2, 4, 6),
   label = c("a","b","c")
 )
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, label = label)) +
   xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)
p + geom_line() + opts(title = "geom_line")
### Message with no plot:
geom_path: Every group consistents of only one observation. Do you
need to adjust the group aesthetic?
                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^

I fixed the typo (see the attachment) but the problem is due to the
presence of the label aesthetic, since each of the following work:

## These all work:
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() + opts(title = 'geom_line')
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() + opts(title = 'geom_line') +
xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL)

These two lines also produce empty plots => the problem is not limited
to geom_path:

p + geom_area() + opts(title = "geom_area")
p + geom_polygon() + opts(title = "geom_polygon")

#####################################
## Issue 3: Just pointing this out re alpha():

td <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(table, depth)) +
   xlim(50, 70) + ylim(50, 70)
jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.5)
## No effect:
td + geom_jitter(position = jit, colour = alpha("black", 1/50))

## Works:
td + geom_jitter(position = jit, alpha = 1/50)

## Issue 4: Colour/color infelicities in opts():

### This needs to get fixed (or Brandon will be apoplectic :):

> hgram + opts(panel.grid.major = theme_line(colour = "red")) # works
> hgram + opts(panel.grid.major = theme_line(color = "red"))
Error in theme_line(color = "red") : unused argument(s) (color = "red")

I may be able to fix this - what needs to be done to make color and
colour equivalent as arguments in a theme_*() function?

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Layers package
messages.body_plain:
I imagine this diagram useful for the dilettante reader more than the
package author (who has internalised the framework in the creation
process). I find that, even though each function has a fairly
self-descriptive name, it's quite hard to keep track of what's going
on when I dig into the source code of these packages.
To me it's a bit like looking at individual pieces of a jigsaw puzzle:
I can see that this particular piece fits with this one to form some
shape, but where did I see the one the should go right here? Also,
what is the big picture again? I need that visual map+index.
This is perhaps because each function performs a relatively small task
(a good thing), which means that in order to get from the general task
to the lower level you have to follow a string of intermediate
functions, somewhat delocalised. That track is what the links between
boxes would represent (they're not necessarily arrows with a
direction). In such a diagram I'd like each box (major function) to
have an input, an output, and its description should be a task.

I'll see if something useful emerges after a few iterations (I realise
now that "layer" should rather be enclosing all the rest; some boxes
should be isolated, etc.)

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Aside from the details of implementation, as of now I have one
question about general design of geom.

How are the inside and outside aes different?

For example, in geom_path, linetype is defined as aesthetic parameter
while lineend etc. is not.
Is the any general and consistent rules for these separations?

Also, param in data, param in inside aes, and param in outside aes
will make confusion:

> df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, width = 1:10/10)
> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white")), df) # width = 1:10/10
> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white"), width = 1), df) # width = 1:10/10
> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white", width = 1)), df) # width = 1

It looks like that the priority is:
inside aes > data > outside aes.
Is this the rule?

OK, what I want to ask is that, why we need the outside-aes
parameters, such as width in bar or lineend in path?

--

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,

> Aside from the details of implementation, as of now I have one
> question about general design of geom.
>
> How are the inside and outside aes different?
>
> For example, in geom_path, linetype is defined as aesthetic parameter
> while lineend etc. is not.
> Is the any general and consistent rules for these separations?

Generally, anything outside aes can't vary with individual elements -
lineend etc are global parameters that affect every line drawn by the
geom.  It's also partly personal preference - the fewer things in the
aesthetics and the more things that are constant, the simple the code
is (and hopefully also faster).

> Also, param in data, param in inside aes, and param in outside aes
> will make confusion:
>
>> df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, width = 1:10/10)
>> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white")), df) # width = 1:10/10
>> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white"), width = 1), df) # width = 1:10/10
>> geom_plot(geom_bar(list(colour = "white", width = 1)), df) # width = 1

Yes, that is confusing - but I it's because it's a bug. Width is an
aesthetic and so shouldn't be a parameter.

> It looks like that the priority is:
> inside aes > data > outside aes.
> Is this the rule?

The rule is aes > data.  There shouldn't be any cases where we have
both inside and outside aes -

> OK, what I want to ask is that, why we need the outside-aes
> parameters, such as width in bar or lineend in path?

These are generally for things that aren't aesthetics, or
can't/shouldn't/don't vary across rows in the data.  I'm still
thinking about this so your feedback is really useful - I definitely
want to end up with a simpler design but more flexibly than the
current.

Also, I'm currently thinking that the layers package will be broken up
in the geom, stat and adjust pieces - they don't really have much in
common, and the idea of a layer is really quite ggplot2 specific.
(The other purpose of breaking ggplot2 up into pieces is so other
graphics packages can pick and choose and implement their own
frameworks)

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Layers package
messages.body_plain:
> Another question is how do coord and geom interacts in premunch?
>
> If I correctly understand, coordinate transformation needs to take
> place after munch, before or during geom_draw.

Correct - but the layers package knows nothing about coordinate
systems or munching so it wouldn't be done in geom_plot, but in
whatever is using the layers package.

> In most cases, actual drawing codes would depend on the coordinate system.
> Probably this would make separating geom such a difficult task.

The idea of geom_premunch is to get the data/geom into a form where
munching is easy - you can assume there is a line connecting each row
(separated by groups), so all munching needs to do is break each line
up into many small pieces and individually transform each location.

In other words, I only know how to munch points, lines and polygons,
so geom_premunch should convert any geom into either geom_point,
geom_line or geom_polygon, by transforming the data appropriately.

Hadley

> It only takes care about how the plot looks to eye. So, in essence,
> decoration is not a part of visualization.

I think that's an overly strict definition of visualisation - I'd say
that decoration is a part of visualisation for two reasons:

(1) Decoration can help improve the perception of a graphic.  For
example, grid lines are decoration, but they do improve the perception
of change and make comparisons easier (I'm not sure if this has been
experimentally verified but Cleveland has a paper that mentions it)

(2) Accurate perception of values (or comparison of values) is not the
only purpose of visualisation.  It's what you're mainly interested in
for exploratory graphics, but expository/communication graphics are
equally important.  Decoration is really important when you are using
a graphic to help people understand a complicated subject.

> These are quite interesting topic for me, because it refers how people
> visually understand abstract (numeric) data, but completely off-topic
> :-p
> Someday I may do experiments and write a paper on this topic in
> conjunction with cognitive science study... someday.

That would be great.  I've been trying to learn more about cognitive
science so I can run the experiments myself.  Last semester I worked
with an undergraduate to do some experiments on mechnical turk to
attempt to generate an ordering of aesthetics for discrete variables -
i.e. which aesthetics form groups most strongly.  I even have a
half-written R package that makes it easier to do experiments on
amazon MTurk.  One day I'd like to get to the point where I can start
an experiment running over night, analyse the results in the morning,
and then have an improved version of the experiment running by the
next evening.

> I agree with the concept. As the structure of aes and other parameters

>
> then it will be more obvious that arrow, lineend, etc are parameter
> for decoration.

Hmmmmmmm, I'm not sure I see a big advantage in doing it this way.
Most geoms will have few additional parameters, and making decoration
a separate list makes it a pain to (e.g.) set lineend = "round"
without setting the other decorations.

Hadley

a data.frame as input). I attach a script that tries to conform better
with the prototype of annotation_raster in ggplot2. Would
